Mozart's other symphonies. Before composing his final three masterpieces in 1788, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote dozens of symphonies, officially numbered 1 to 38, though some are spurious and others exist outside the numbering. These works track his growth from a child prodigy writing Italian-style symphonies to a mature artist in Salzburg and Vienna.

Symphony No. 25 in G minor, known as the "Little" G minor, was written when Mozart was seventeen under the influence of the Sturm und Drang, or Storm and Stress movement. Its syncopated opening horn blasts are famous for scoring the opening sequence of the film Amadeus. Moving forward to his later Viennese symphonies, Symphony No. 38 in D major is nicknamed the Prague to honor the city where it premiered in 1787. Unusually for a late classical symphony, it has only three movements, completely omitting the standard minuet and trio.

Symphony No. 36 in C major is called the Linz because Mozart composed it in just four days during a stopover in the town of Linz to prepare for an unexpected concert. It is his first symphony to feature a slow opening introduction. The Haffner Symphony, No. 35 in D major, was commissioned by the Salzburg Haffner family to celebrate Sigmund Haffner's ennoblement.

Earlier in his career, Symphony No. 29 in A major is an elegant chamber-like work written in Salzburg in 1774, marked by a soaring, octave-leaping opening theme in the violins. Symphony No. 31 in D major is the Paris, composed during a job-seeking trip to the French capital in 1778. This work is notable for its large orchestra and for being the first time Mozart incorporated clarinets in a symphony.

These earlier symphonies laid the structural foundation for his final three symphonies, and they demonstrate how the same Sturm und Drang movement that influenced Symphony No. 25 was a parallel trend in literature and painting emphasizing intense, dramatic emotion.
